dehydrated_text:
It was just a bad essay. My teachers liked me but they really didn't like me because I seemed aggressive to them. You know, I wanted grades too much; they use the word "ambitious." They thought I was ambitious. In Canada, ambition is seen as a dirty word—it means not playing by the rules, being too aggressive, or pushy.

This is my application to Yale, which is decent but still needs improvement. How did I get in? Because there was some information from the application that made them interested in me. Firstly, I was poor and couldn't afford the application fee; I had to apply for a waiver.

I was born in China in 1976 and moved with my family to Canada in 1983 when I was six. So, I was a poor immigrant. I transferred from a poor high school to a rich one, switching neighborhoods. My family lived in a poor area, but I spent half an hour each day on the subway going to the new school.

Canadians don't like such transfers; they want you to stay where you are. When I told my principal about transferring, he got upset and threatened to write a discipline letter that would follow me to university applications, which is very serious.

When I went to the rich high school, I had no friends because people didn't like new arrivals. I was ambitious but desperate due to my family's poverty. They knew I was an average student who was pushy and ambitious, factors that led Yale to accept me as it saw my dissociative personality disorder—desperation to survive, insecurity, transgressiveness in breaking rules for success.

Desperation means if I didn't get into Yale, I would drown; insecurity means always needing more achievements. I wasn't moral; I broke the rule of not leaving my poor school for a rich one. I ignored the principal and went anyway, telling everyone I was going to get good grades and enter the Ivy League.

Yale saw these traits—desperation, insecurity, hunger, immorality—and that's why they let me in because it’s possible I might go crazy.
